cards.title: Single-exponential dependence on dimension for integer programming
cards.formal: Do constants C,c>0 and a deterministic algorithm exist that decide whether Ax≤b has an integer solution x∈ℤ^n in at most 2^(Cn)(L+1)^c bit operations, for every rational matrix A and vector b?
cards.definitions: Use uniform classical deterministic Turing computation, with no advice or oracle. Integers and rational numerators and denominators are encoded in binary; L denotes the total input bit length. A polynomial bound has constants independent of the input. A has m rows and n columns, both dimensions are part of the input, and the system need not be bounded. No limit on coefficient size, number of constraints or lattice width is promised. This target concerns feasibility.

context_blocks.text: Integer programming is polynomial-time solvable in every fixed dimension, but the dependence on dimension determines how far that tractability extends. The single-exponential target would make the geometric dimension cost comparable to exhaustive search over a constant-size choice per variable.

The 2025 survey records the Reis–Rothvoss bound (log n)^{O(n)}·poly(L) and explicitly identifies 2^{O(n)}·poly(L) as open. Here n is the number of integer variables, not the coefficient bit length. The question applies to unrestricted systems rather than one block-structured subclass.

cards.formal: Historical question, resolved negatively under ETH: can integer-programming feasibility Ax=b, x∈ℤⁿ_{≥0}, for an arbitrary integer m×n matrix A and integer m-vector b, be decided by a deterministic algorithm in time (m n Δ)^{o(m)} B^{O(1)}, or even in time (m n Δ B)^{o(m)}? cards.definitions:
Inputs have m,n≥1, A∈ℤ^{m×n} and b∈ℤ^m, encoded by dimensions and the full signed binary lists of their entries. Let L be this total bit length. A YES instance has some vector x with n nonnegative integer entries satisfying every equality ∑ⱼ Aᵢⱼxⱼ=bᵢ; no upper bounds on x are supplied. A NO instance has no such vector. The task is exact decision of feasibility, with no objective vector and no approximation or real-valued relaxation. Ordinary deterministic Turing bit complexity is used, with worst-case time on the given parameters. Matrix coefficients may be negative; the resolution already holds for the nonnegative 0/1 subclass.

The first proposed bound means that one algorithm and constants C,c≥1 and a function g:ℕ→ℝ_{≥0} exist with g(m)/m→0 as m→∞, such that for every input its running time is at most C L^c (2mnΔ)^{g(m)} (2B)^c. The second means that one algorithm, constants C,c≥1 and such a function g exist with time at most C L^c (2mnΔB)^{g(m)} on every input. The exponent function and constants do not depend on n, A or b. Explicit factors 2 and clamping Δ,B at 1 remove degenerate zero or unit bases. A fixed polynomial factor in binary input length is allowed, making the lower-bound claim stronger and avoiding an implicit free input-reading convention. This does not permit an arbitrary factor depending on m. Any first-form bound is also a second-form bound after adding a constant to g; a second-form bound need not have only polynomial dependence on B.

ETH is the deterministic Exponential Time Hypothesis: satisfiability of Boolean 3-CNF formulas with N variables and encoding length M has no deterministic algorithm of time 2^{o(N)} M^{O(1)}. A 3-CNF is a conjunction of clauses with at most three literals each. The result is the implication from this hypothesis to nonexistence of the stated IP algorithms; it is not an unconditional time lower bound and does not replace ETH by its randomized analogue.

In the later theorem, the row and column parameters are named k and ℓ; they correspond to this card’s m and n. Theorem 1 restricts to A∈{0,1}^{m×n}, b∈ℕ^m, with n and ||b||∞ at most a universal constant times m log(m+2). It excludes time 2^{o(m log(m+2))} under ETH. On this restricted family, L is polynomial in m and each of the two proposed runtimes is 2^{o(m log(m+2))}; the extra L^c and polynomial B factor do not avoid the lower bound. Corollary 2 of the revised full text additionally puts b in {0,1}^m while allowing A entries in {−1,0,1}.
cards.answer_criterion: The requested historical negative result is a proof that either proposed deterministic running-time bound implies failure of ETH, with the stated parameter dependencies. Theorem 1 establishes this already on the restricted 0/1-matrix family described above, and hence for the general problem. The result does not establish ETH itself or exclude bounded-error randomized algorithms under deterministic ETH alone.
